content.text:
`out/module.ts` is written and type-checks. It keeps lodash behaviour, but the bundle is 1962 bytes min+gzip, up from 550 in the first draft. The 1962 bytes come from the one function that needs `es-toolkit/compat`.

`npm run size` reports 113 bytes of my own code. I couldn't get a number for the original, because `lodash` isn't installed in this project and `src/module.ts` fails to build. I didn't install anything.

I read the declarations and source of the installed es-toolkit (1.53.2) and chose these functions:

- **`applyPatch`**: `merge` from `es-toolkit/object`. It deep-merges in place and returns the target, and arrays merge by index, as in lodash. On a nested sample with arrays of objects, `null` values and new keys, it gave the same result as `compat.merge`.
- **`toLookup`**: `zipObject` from `es-toolkit/array`, with a small `map` adapter to split the pairs into keys and values. Duplicate names keep the last value, as `fromPairs` does.
- **`toTitle`**: `startCase` from `es-toolkit/compat`, not from `es-toolkit/string`. The main `startCase` lowercases acronyms, so `"AB-_Y03A1"` gives `"Ab Y 03 A 1"`. Lodash gives `"AB Y 03 A 1"`, and the input range explicitly allows consecutive capitals. The main version differed from the compat one on about 22% of 200,000 random strings built from letters, digits and separators. The compat version keeps case and reproduces the known lodash result on my sample.

No lodash import is left. The compat `startCase` is the only es-toolkit function I found that preserves the behaviour for those inputs. I couldn't compare against real lodash, so I used `es-toolkit/compat` as the reference for lodash behaviour. That is why the compat `startCase` is trusted here, and why I checked its output by hand against known lodash results.
